title: Workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16)
hookLine: those hired at the last hour get a full day's pay, and the early ones grumble

cards: Dawn, in a village square. Men wait, hoping for a day's work. A landowner hires a crew for his vineyard, and they agree the usual wage: one silver coin, a day's pay.
At nine he's back for more. At noon, more. At three, more.
At five, with one hour of light left, men are still standing there. Why are you idle all day? Because no one hired us.
So he sends them in too. At sunset the pay line forms, and he tells his manager: start with the last. The five o'clock crew each get one silver coin, a full day's pay for one hour.

teach.h: THEY HAVE A POINT. IT ISN'T FAIR.
teach.b: The complaint, in the King James, is hard to argue with: "These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day." They have a point.
It isn't fair, and the owner doesn't pretend it is. He says: friend, I did you no wrong; you agreed to a coin.

teach.h: IS THINE EYE EVIL, BECAUSE I AM GOOD?
teach.b: Then a sharp question: "is thine eye evil, because I am good?" Why does my generosity to them feel like a loss to you? Christians read it more than one way.
Some hear grace: God's welcome isn't a wage earned by the hour, and someone who comes to faith on their last day is welcomed like someone who came as a child.
Others hear who belongs: old insiders and newcomers made equal.

teach.h: GRACE, BELONGING, A FULL DAY'S PAY.
teach.b: Some notice the money: one coin was the day's wage they all agreed on, so the latecomers go home with a full day's pay, like everyone else. Churches hold these readings side by side.
And the English phrase the eleventh hour, for just in time, is often traced to this crew, hired at the eleventh hour of the working day.

teach.h: A WEEK OF STORIES THAT OVERPAY.
teach.b: That closes a week of stories: why he told them at all, seed on every ground, a mustard seed and a pinch of yeast, a shepherd after one sheep, a woman sweeping for one coin, a treasure worth everything, and now a boss who pays the last first.
In almost every one, somebody gives more than makes sense.

how: Christians often read this parable as a picture of God's grace, given the same to people who come to faith late as to those who came early. It's a common text for sermons on envy, fairness and welcome.

o: a silver coin, a laborer's pay for one day
a gold coin worth a whole season of work
a tax paid to Rome after each harvest

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: bore the burden and heat of the day
one hour, a full day's pay
is thine eye evil, because I am good?
one silver coin, a day's wage

s: the owner cheats the early workers
they get exactly what they agreed to. the owner says: friend, I do thee no wrong.
the last crew is hired at the eleventh hour
about one hour of light is left. the English phrase "the eleventh hour" is often traced to them.
everyone reads this story the same way
some hear grace, others hear insiders and newcomers made equal, and some notice that everyone goes home with a day's pay.

games.q: you're the owner at sunset. the dawn crew are angry that the five o'clock crew got the same coin. what do you say?
o: fine. next time the late ones get less.
friend, I did you no wrong. is your eye evil because I am good?
games.why: he doesn't pretend it's fair. he says they got what they agreed to, and asks why his generosity feels like their loss.

practice: Think of the ledger you carry: who does the dishes, who texted last, who got the credit, who got off easy. Find one line and, without erasing it, feel what keeping it costs you.
If you pray, hand it to God; if not, loosen your grip, a little.

wordCard.voice: Denarius. The silver coin, a full day's wage, that every worker goes home with, hired at dawn or at the eleventh hour.

orig.note: Greek, from the Latin denarius: a silver coin, a laborer's day's pay. the old King James calls it a penny.

carryVoice: Your line: generosity isn't fair. it's better. A week of stories, wrapped; see you on day twenty-nine.
